html:
A battle fought in northeast Gaul, in today's France, in June 451, in which a Roman and Visigothic army stopped the Huns under Attila. The Roman general Flavius Aetius led a coalition in which Germanic allies made up most of the troops, above all the Visigoths under their king Theodoric I, who was killed in the fighting. Attila's army included Ostrogoths, Gepids and other subject peoples.

Attila had crossed the Rhine in spring and besieged Orléans, but drew back when Aetius came up. The battle, somewhere near Châlons or Troyes, was very bloody and ended without a clear result: Attila withdrew to his wagon camp and then back across the Rhine. The next year he invaded Italy instead. He died in 453, and his empire broke up soon after.

It was one of the last great campaigns of the Western Roman Empire, which now needed barbarian allies to fight barbarian invaders. Older histories called it a battle that saved Western civilisation; most historians now see it as less decisive, with the relief of Orléans the real turning point. It sits under Central Asia on this chart because the Huns came out of the steppe.
